title: From Anger to Contempt: The Emotional Pathways to Satisfaction Loss and Divorce in Romantic Relationships
abstract: ABSTRACT Having a satisfying intimate relationship is a key predictor of happiness and emotional well‐being, yet conflict is an inevitable aspect of romantic life. Different emotions play a central role in shaping how partners experience and manage conflict and may have distinct relational consequences. The present research includes three studies examining the differential roles of anger and contempt in romantic conflict. Drawing on prior work suggesting that anger may serve adaptive functions whereas contempt is more destructive, we investigated their motivational, behavioral, and relational implications. In Study 1 ( N = 276), participants recalled a conflict in which they felt either anger or contempt toward their partner. Anger was associated with verbal attack and coercion, which in turn were weakly and positively associated with relationship satisfaction, whereas contempt was linked to partner derogation and social exclusion, which were associated with lower satisfaction. Study 2 ( N = 363) replicated these findings across diverse conflict types, showing that anger was mainly associated with verbal attack and coercion goals but not with divorce intentions, whereas past and current contempt were associated with partner derogation, social exclusion, lower relationship quality, and stronger divorce intentions. Study 3 experimentally induced romantic conflict in 60 couples. Severe conflicts uniquely amplified contempt—but not anger—and post‐conflict contempt was strongly predicted by pre‐existing levels of anger and contempt, suggesting that contempt responses may reflect accumulated emotional dispositions rather than reactions to the conflict at hand. Together, these findings underscore the importance of distinguishing discrete negative emotions in romantic conflict and highlight the particularly harmful role of contempt in relationship deterioration.
